newsitem.title: USA: U.S. targets farm trade monopolies in talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. targets farm trade monopolies in talks.

text.p: Reform of farm monopolies in China and the former Soviet republics, along with marketing boards in Canada, Australia and New Zealand will be a U.S. priority in the next round of world trade negotiations, Deputy Agriculture Secretary Richard Rominger said Thursday.
A summit by national trade leaders this winter will lay the framework for the global talks due to begin in 1999. The United States has highlighted the issue of state trading enterprises (STEs).
"If we are to continue to phase out (farm) export subsidies, we need equivalent disciplines on STEs and related trade-distorting practices," Rominger told the House Agriculture Committee.

U.S. officials say state trading enterprises, which often enjoy monopoly control over the export of a commodity and operate in secret, can offer unfairly low prices in order to win sales. Other state trading enterprises can artificially drive up domestic prices by muzzling imports.

While referring to longstanding U.S. concerns with the export dealings of the Canadian Wheat Board, Australian Wheat Board and New Zealand Dairy Board, Rominger said state trading enterprises also were a cause for concern in China and former Soviet republics.
He said trade practices must be brought under control before the latter nations could join the World Trade Organisation.

Thirty nations have told the World Trade Organisation that a total of 121 state trading enterprises were involved in their agricultural trade. The enterprises were active in grain, dairy, cotton, livestock, meat, oilseeds, horticultural products and some tropical products.
In a statement to the hearing, the New Zealand Dairy Board said it was a fair trader. It said its profits from sales to the United States stemmed from artificially high U.S. prices.

U.S. farm groups have generally backed the Clinton administration in its drive to control the state trading bodies. The American Farm Bureau Federation, the largest of the groups, said "we must put China at the top of the list" for use of state trading enterprises to block imports.

The National Farmers Union said elimination of state trading groups would benefit grain processors and exporters while forcing down prices paid to farmers. An end to Canada's Wheat Board, it said, would mean a deluge of grain onto the U.S. market.
